Questions and answers

The questions families ask most. If yours is not here, ask the person who runs your course.

More questions

Do I need to know anything about computers to follow tonight?
No. Every technical word is explained, and you never need to code to help your child.

About the evening

Will the slides be shared?
Yes: hand out the one-page summary; the full slides with references are available on request.

Why now

Will coding guarantee my child a good job?
No, and nobody can promise that. What we can say is that understanding how computers and AI work is becoming a basic literacy, like understanding money or science.
Does our local school teach coding?
It varies a lot by school. It is worth asking; our course works alongside school, not instead of it.
Should my child use ChatGPT for homework?
Not for this course. The homework is about thinking through the problem; we teach how AI works in Level 3 instead.

The research

So will it help with math?
Possibly a little, and especially with problem solving, but we do not promise better math grades. Think of it as its own valuable subject.
What is “thinking about thinking”?
Metacognition: noticing how you are solving a problem and changing strategy when it isn’t working. Debugging practices exactly this.
Is 0.89 a lot?
Yes, it is large by usual standards, but it comes from a small number of studies, so treat it as promising rather than proven.
Why show a study of six-year-olds?
Because it is one of the few truly randomized trials. Studies of older children mostly point the same way but with weaker designs.
My daughter says coding is for boys. What can I do?
Encourage her as much as you would a son, and point out the variety of people who code. Our course never assigns roles by gender.
Then why bother?
Because coding is worth learning for its own sake, like music or a language, and because the way we teach it (projects, teamwork, debugging) builds good learning habits.

How we teach

Is there one best way to teach coding?
No single method wins everywhere, but these ingredients are consistently linked to better learning and motivation.
My child only wants to make games. Is that OK?
Yes. Games are a great vehicle: they need loops, conditions, variables and debugging. Art and data projects are there for others.
What if my child does not get along with their partner?
We rotate pairs, set clear roles and swap every few minutes. With an odd number, a trio uses driver, navigator and tester.
Isn’t time away from the computer wasted?
No. Off-screen activities make the ideas concrete and give eyes a break; they are short and always lead into building.

The course

What if my child is ahead or behind the others?
Every lesson has an easier route and a stretch challenge, and two optional spare sessions per level give time to catch up within the 12 weeks.
Isn’t Scratch just a toy?
It is a real programming language with the same core ideas; we use it as a ramp, and move to Python after six weeks.
Do we have to commit to all three levels?
No. Each level ends with a complete project and a certificate; you decide about the next level then.
Is typing a problem for a ten-year-old?
Programs at this level are short; we start very small, and typing improves quickly.
What if my child struggled with Level 1?
The placement quiz and Level 1 review show where to start; repeating parts of Level 1 is completely fine.
Isn’t this too advanced for 11-year-olds?
It is challenging by design, with step-by-step support. By Level 3 the children have 20 to 24 weeks of practice behind them.
We don’t have a Mac at home. Is that a problem?
No. Paper parts of the homework work at the kitchen table, and computer tasks can be finished at the next session.
Will I get a report?
You will see the project at each showcase and can ask for the checkpoint and rubric results; there is also a progress tracker children fill in.

Helping at home

What if my child asks me for help and I don’t know the answer?
Perfect: say “Let’s find out.” Ask them to explain the code line by line; they often spot the bug themselves.

Safety and privacy

Will my child’s photo or work be posted online?
No. Showcases happen on screen at home, and nothing is uploaded.

Common concerns

What if my child loses interest?
It happens. Children choose their projects, which helps, and each level is a natural stopping point.
Is this better than an online course?
Different: a small group, a familiar adult, no accounts, and a lot of talking and pair work, which research supports.
Can siblings join?
The group is up to four children so everyone gets attention; ask, and we will see what is possible.

Kids Coding

A free course for children from Grade 5: make games and art, first with Scratch blocks, then with Python. One 60-minute session a week.

No accounts, no ads, no tracking.
